items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: I always felt that the earliest books of Robert Goffin’s book in Belgium were rather skimpy

ctx.x: Yes certainly it was before LPs, but the idea of him spreading through recording.

Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following month, and that way they were on the lookout. And the annotations that I wrote for the 78 RPM albums were the first group of written documentation of the careers of some of these performers, because before that there…

rather special reason that I didn’t catch on to at first, which was that the American jazz records that got released abroad tended to stay in the catalogues. They didn’t sell very widely and the record business was smaller in Europe than it was in America, and because they stayed in the catalogues they were there for reference as more and more people got interested in the historical recordings of the 1920s and early 30s. items.q: They captured interest in such a way that the very first book on jazz was written by a Belgian, Robert Goffin, and the second book, which was substantially better, was written by Hughes Panassié.

ctx.x: manager had said something like, “Yes, we had a letter from somebody suggesting some specific reissues that we ought to put out.” It turned out, when he pulled out the letter, that it was the letter that I had written several months before. I guess it was the early fall of 1939, or maybe even earlier. I have a way of finding out when it was, because I got an answer from the plant manager, and I happened to save the answer and came across it a few months ago. The date is right on there. listing – in addition to the catalog number, they listed each side as Rhythm Style Series number 1 and 2, on one record, 3 and 4 on another record. They put out a lot of these records, but they had some bizarre couplings. They would couple Miff Mole and his Molers with Louis Armstrong on the other side. The periods also seemed to jump around.
